sweep_summary: One stress-title item for Ge'ez: Trumpp 1874 'Ueber den Accent im Aethiopischen' (ZDMG 28: 515-561). It is fully open on archive.org (DLI copy of ZDMG 28; the scanned text was already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass, and today the volume PDF was downloaded and the article's 47 pages extracted to; written there; pp. 520-521 verified against the page scan). It is squarely about Ge'ez word accent in the traditional pronunciation, elicited first-hand in 1870-73, and it is the primary source behind the catalog's Gragg 1997 / Dillmann 1907 statements. It confirms the 'morphological' coding (accent set by the word's morphological formation and word class, not by vowel length; verb penult, 2 f. pl. -kén, nouns with stem-final/ending-determined stress, accusative -a toneless) and refines it with a three-syllable window (antepenult only for three open short syllables with medial ə) and a weight/guttural component inside the noun rules. Recommendation: keep Gragg 1997 as the deciding modern statement, add Trumpp 1874 pp. 520-521, 525, 531, 547 to the record as the primary first-hand evidence; nothing remains to acquire (a cleaner scan from MENAdoc/Halle would be cosmetic; the MENAdoc search URL now redirects to menalib.de and was not pursued). The Priess 2022 Aethiopica review already in the folder is not a stress item and contains no stress remarks.

new_statements.quote: Der Accent ist im Aethiopischen nicht an die langen Vocale als solche gebunden, sondern richtet sich vielmehr nach der Bildung des einzelnen Wortes. Viel wichtiger als ein langer Vocal ist für den Wortton ein Hauchlaut, der [...] den Ton an sich zu ziehen bestrebt ist. Allgemein giltige Regeln lassen sich daher über den Wortton im Aethiopischen kaum aufstellen, sondern derselbe muss an den einzelnen Bildungen nachgewiesen werden, wobei sich das Verbum wieder wesentlich vom Nomen unterscheidet, da es seine eigenen Ton-Geseze hat.
new_statements.translation: In Ethiopic the accent is not bound to the long vowels as such, but is governed rather by the formation of the individual word. Far more important for word stress than a long vowel is a guttural, which [...] strives to draw the stress to itself. Generally valid rules for word stress in Ethiopic can therefore hardly be set up; it must instead be demonstrated for each individual formation, and here the verb differs essentially from the noun, since it has its own stress laws.

new_statements.reading: The primary first-hand record of the traditional pronunciation (1870-73 elicitation from a Gondar-trained däbtära and a Falasha informant), on which the later summaries rest. It supports the catalog's 'morphological' coding directly: stress position is set by the morphological formation and word class (verb vs noun have separate laws), not by vowel length or syllable count. It refines the catalog in three ways: (1) a hard three-syllable window with antepenult stress only in words of three open short syllables with medial ə (otherwise penult); (2) within nouns, a weight component (a long or positionally long vowel in a disyllable takes stress; two long syllables stress the last) plus guttural attraction, matching the Dillmann 1907 sec. 59 'heavy' note already in the record; (3) explicit confirmation of the details Gragg 1997 gives: perfect penult (nabára), 2 f. pl. nagarkén final, plurals nagáru (against Ludolf/Dillmann's nagarú), accusative -a unstressed (zánta, aḥáda). No contradiction of the current classification.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations (Gragg 1997 p. 246; Dillmann/Crichton 1907 sec. 59) are present verbatim at the stated places in the held archive.org text layers. (2) Deciding source: a 1997 handbook grammar sketch by the field's Ge‘ez phonologist, explicitly summarizing the traditional-pronunciation literature (Leslau 1987, Mittwoch 1926, Makonnen 1984); secondary support from the 1907 reference grammar. Newly downloaded Trumpp 1874 (ZDMG 28, the fieldwork-based accent study Dillmann's translator prefers) independently states that Ge‘ez accent is not bound to vowel length but 'richtet sich nach der Bildung des einzelnen Wortes', that verb and noun have separate accent laws, perfect = penult, verb-final never stressed: this confirms set by morphology. (3) Better sources exist but are not yet obtained (Tropper & Hasselbach-Andee 2021 reference grammar, 440 pp; Mittwoch 1926; Gragg in Kaye 199

sources.quote: p. 520: "Der Accent ist im Aethiopischen nicht an die langen Vocale als solche gebunden, sondern richtet sich vielmehr nach der Bildung des einzelnen Wortes. Viel wichtiger als ein langer Vocal ist für den Wortton ein Hauchlaut, der, wo es die Wortbildung nur immer zulässt, den Ton an sich zu ziehen bestrebt ist. Allgemein giltige Regeln lassen sich daher über den Wortton im Aethiopischen kaum aufstellen, sondern derselbe muss an den einzelnen Bildungen nachgewiesen werden, wobei sich das Verbum wieder wesentlich vom Nomen unterscheidet, da es seine eigenen Ton-Geseze hat." p. 521: "Hier gilt als Grundregel, dass der Ton auf der penultima ruht."

sources.note: First-hand documentation of Ge'ez word accent in the traditional (Abyssinian scholarly) pronunciation, elicited in 1870-73 from a Falasha informant and the Gondar-trained däbtära Walda Sellase (pp. 515-516). General principle (p. 520): accent is not bound to long vowels but set by the morphological formation of each word; a guttural (Hauchlaut) attracts stress wherever the morphology permits; no generally valid rules, only rules per formation; verb and noun have separate accent laws; accent never spans more than the last three syllables (barákata impossible); antepenult only when the word has…
